articles.title: Fair play: on a hurried delimitation of Lok Sabha constituencies
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: The government must build consensus on delimitation

The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) appears to have zeroed in on a hurried delimitation of Lok Sabha constituencies as the central piece of its strategy for the next general election, due in 2029. As the current constitutional scheme stands, a fresh delimitation is triggered once the data from the ongoing Census 2027 is published . That default path, which is based on population distribution across States, will considerably cut down the representation of States that have stabilised their population since the last delimitation. The Centre has now proposed to extend the constitutional freeze on inter-State distribution of Lok Sabha seats for another 25 years, until 2051, while increasing the size of the House to a maximum of 850 seats. The demarcation of the boundaries of Lok Sabha constituencies will be based on the 2011 Census within each State. The delimitation exercise will also bring into force 33% reservation for women , which Parliament approved in 2023. Considering the need to balance the ‘one person, one vote’ principle with the principles of federalism, which is about protecting the group rights of States, the proposals are a reasonable way forward for India. That said, the inter-State distribution of Lok Sabha seats is such a central question of democracy and federalism that any changes must be preceded by thoughtful deliberations at multiple levels.

That makes the approach of the Centre , which is trying to pass a constitutional amendment through defections and manipulations, dubious and lacking in good faith. If the Centre has been willing to extend the constitutional guarantee of inter-State distribution of seats on the basis of the 1971 Census, it could have built an all-party consensus on the issue . Instead, in April, it made a deceptive move by promising to maintain the current proportion of seats while the constitutional amendment it moved would have made that promise unconstitutional. At present, when the Centre is keen to appear accommodative, a more appropriate manner to proceed with such a generational measure in India’s federal democracy is to refer the Bills to a parliamentary committee that can examine them in detail and generate a national conversation. A bigger Lok Sabha will create its own challenges , while the case for increasing its size is not entirely without merit as India’s population has grown by at least 2.6 times since the 1971 Census, which forms the basis of the last delimitation of 1973, based on the 1971 Census. The Centre should not rush this vital question, which is not merely about garnering enough votes for passing a Bill. It must be based on consensus, as it happened in 1976 and again in 2001, under a Prime Minister from the Congress and one from the BJP, respectively.

articles.title: Lifting off: on China’s launch of Pakistan’s first astronaut
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Science-based diplomacy could aid India-Pakistan bilateral engagement

The economic and diplomatic consequences of India’s efforts to estrange Pakistan often overshadow the costs distributed between them. For example, Pakistani space scientists can today access facilities in China whereas Indian space scientists can access facilities in the United States and Europe . But Indian scientists studying environmental conditions in Pakistan and Pakistani scientists studying conditions in India have far fewer alternatives. The latter matters much more for regional development and stability. On November 25, Beijing’s ‘Space Silk Road’ diplomacy and the strain on New Delhi’s hedging strategies converged in the Shenzhou-24 mission as China launched Pakistan’s first astronaut , Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, to the Tiangong space station. Pakistan had offered in 2015 to contribute to India’s proposed SAARC satellite and wanted the project administered under SAARC, but India insisted on operating it as largesse to its neighbours. If it had really been SAARC’s satellite, ISRO and its Pakistani counterpart, SUPARCO , could have developed an institutional relationship and India could have influenced its neighbour’s space programme through a multilateral mechanism. But today, India’s ability to engage Pakistan on regional matters has increasingly depended on negotiating with powers beyond South Asia, in institutions with other agendas.

Even as spaceflight emerges as a new geopolitical realm, its substantial scientific component affords countries opportunities to engage independently of interstate relations in other domains. The Shenzhou-24 experience will be significant for SUPARCO just as the Axiom-4 mission in the U.S. was for ISRO , helping to significantly lower Islamabad’s cost to access similar future opportunities, especially those under the Asia-Pacific Space Cooperation Organization, which also includes Bangladesh, and the Belt and Road Initiative’s Space Information Corridor . There is no question that Indian spaceflight is technologically superior to that of Pakistan, but the Shenzhou-24 mission is a reminder that China’s technological superiority vis-à-vis India’s leaves India with an unequal contest. India has been ceding the neighbourhood to China’s space networks, and by squandering the opportunities afforded by science diplomacy, it has left Pakistan to look to China even on problems it shares with India. The Apollo-Soyuz interaction during the Cold War and India and Pakistan working together to respond to a locust outbreak barely a year after the Balakot crisis (2019) are testament to the ability of science-based diplomacy to clear room for bilateral engagement with guardrails, without compromising the counter-terrorism agenda. India should revive such engagement.

For example, Pakistani space scientists can today access facilities in China whereas Indian space scientists can access facilities in the United States and Europe . But Indian scientists studying environmental conditions in Pakistan and Pakistani scientists studying conditions in India have far fewer alternatives. The latter matters much more for regional development and stability. On November 25, Beijing’s ‘Space Silk Road’ diplomacy and the strain on New Delhi’s hedging strategies converged in the Shenzhou-24 mission as China launched Pakistan’s first astronaut , Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, to the Tiangong space station. Pakistan had offered in 2015 to contribute to India’s proposed SAARC satellite and wanted the project administered under SAARC, but India insisted on operating it as largesse to its neighbours. If it had really been SAARC’s satellite, ISRO and its Pakistani counterpart, SUPARCO , could have developed an institutional relationship and India could have influenced its neighbour’s space programme through a multilateral mechanism. But today, India’s ability to engage Pakistan on regional matters has increasingly depended on negotiating with powers beyond South Asia, in institutions with other agendas.
• Even as spaceflight emerges as a new geopolitical realm, its substantial scientific component affords countries opportunities to engage independently of interstate relations in other domains. The Shenzhou-24 experience will be significant for SUPARCO just as the Axiom-4 mission in the U.S. was for ISRO , helping to significantly lower Islamabad’s cost to access similar future opportunities, especially those under the Asia-Pacific Space Cooperation Organization, which also includes Bangladesh, and the Belt and Road Initiative’s Space Information Corridor . There is no question that Indian spaceflight is technologically superior to that of Pakistan, but the Shenzhou-24 mission is a reminder that China’s technological superiority vis-à-vis India’s leaves India with an unequal contest. India has been ceding the neighbourhood to China’s space networks, and by squandering the opportunities afforded by science diplomacy, it has left Pakistan to look to China even on problems it shares with India. The Apollo-Soyuz interaction during the Cold War and India and Pakistan working together to respond to a locust outbreak barely a year after the Balakot crisis (2019) are testament to the ability of science-based diplomacy to clear room for bilateral engagement with guardrails, without compromising the counter-terrorism agenda. India should revive such engagement.

fullParagraphs: Tamil Nadu should have followed Court order without backing Deepathoon claim

By defying the Supreme Court’s one-time direction to also light the ceremonial Karthigai Deepam at a stone pillar , claimed by Hindu groups to be a Deepathoon, atop the Thirupparankundram hills, the Tamil Nadu government has disregarded a constitutional body’s authority. Believed to be Lord Murugan’s first abode, the hills have, for centuries , witnessed an intersection of religious faiths, with occasional skirmishes leading to tense flare-ups and legal battles. They house the Arulmigu Subramaniya Swamy, Uchchi Pillaiyar and Kashi Viswanathar temples; Sultan Sikkandar Avulia Dargah; and also Jain beds. Historically, the lamp is lit near the Pillaiyar temple. In 1994-95, the Hindu Munnani precipitated matters, claiming that the moksha deepam (for departed souls) and Karthigai Deepam were being lit at the same place. It demanded the lamp be lit at a pillar, 50 metres from the Dargah. In multiple legal battles, successive governments, backed by hereditary priests (Sthaneeka Bhattars) , opposed the demand. Even in 1862 and 1912, courts had disallowed lamp lighting near the Dargah. The BJP and its affiliates have, since, aggressively weaponised the demand in the name of Hindu religious rights.

Against this backdrop, last year, the Madras High Cour t’s Madurai Bench, relying on the 1931 Privy Council ruling on ownership of the hills, held that “for the sake of protecting its property, the [Subramania Swamy] temple management is obliged to light the festival lamp at the Deepathoon” . The DMK government defied the order. Later, a Division Bench upheld the verdict. While staying this order recently, the Supreme Court cited the festival’s proximity to permit the lamp to be lit at the Deepathoon this year alone , clarifying that this did not constitute “essential religious practice”. The State filed a review petition , arguing when no right is recognised prima facie, a direction altering the existing position lacks judicial foundation. On Karthigai Deepam day, November 24, with the review pending, the government walked a tightrope. The Collector assured the High Court of compliance. Yet, the lamp was lit only at the traditional spot . The Collector has now apologised to the Court, blaming the temple’s Board of Trustees for not authorising the proposed lighting team at the Deepathoon. The administration has thus attempted to distinguish its proclaimed intent to comply with judicial directions from customs governed by the trustees. But it remains exposed to the charge of colluding with the temple authorities to breach a judicial mandate. The Deepathoon may be a mischievous prop deployed by self-serving Hindu groups, but the pillar stands on temple property. The State could have permitted the limited lighting, leaving the onus on the Court, without endorsing the Deepathoon claim or compromising religious amity. A democracy can remain healthy only when its constitutional pillars do not collide with one another.

articles.title: Pressure tactics: On the new U.S. tariffs on India
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: The new U.S. tariffs must not erode India’s stand on a trade deal

The latest U.S. tariffs on India are nothing more than a pressure tactic to push for the signing of a trade deal. The U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) has proposed to levy a tariff of 25% for India’s apparent use of strategic excess manufacturing capacity to the detriment of American industry. This is the second-highest tariff rate the USTR has applied across the 14 countries that it has taken action against. The pressure on India does not come from the 25% rate but from the 17% this could be reduced to if it signs a trade deal with the U.S. This latest action is yet another example of how, despite the frothiness of India-U.S. trade relations over the past year and a half, the actual substance has not changed. The 25% rate now proposed, which is net of existing tariffs, is nearly the same as the 26% rate that U.S. President Donald Trump had first announced when he unveiled his ‘Liberation Day’ reciprocal tariffs in April 2025. Indeed, it is exactly the same as the 25% tariff he finally imposed in July 2025, before he imposed an additional 25% for India’s Russian oil imports. The 17% rate is also only marginally lower than the 18% that the two countries had agreed on in their joint statement in February 2026. It is also just one percentage point lower than the tariffs on competitors such as Indonesia and Malaysia. The allegation of India having excess capacity does not hold water. Indeed, were India to have excess manufacturing capacity in any sector, it would be the Government of India that would be the first to announce it with great fanfare, instead of denying it as it did. After all, that has been its aim since 2014.

Yet, even a basic assessment of India’s import dependence and the fact that manufacturing’s share in GDP is lower now than a decade ago shows that India is far from having excess manufacturing capacity in any sector. Further, higher tariffs are unlikely to reduce America’s imports of the goods from India that it does depend on. The USTR mentioned generic pharmaceuticals, telecommunication equipment, and renewable energy goods. The first two are items that India has developed expertise in, which is distinct from strategic excess capacity. A relatively small tariff disadvantage will not substantially erode the attractiveness of these Indian products. Renewable energy imports from India have swelled because the U.S. is reducing its purchases from China. Hanging over all of this are the 100% tariffs related to the purchase of Russian oil, which have only temporarily been paused. India has so far held off on signing a deal, and must go ahead with one only if it is convinced that the benefits at least equal the costs.

articles.title: All to play for: On the World chess championship in Geneva
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Chess is one sport where both the young and the old can excel

The World chess championship opened in Geneva with a game worthy of the occasion. Both the defending champion, D. Gukesh, and his challenger, Javokhir Sindarov, produced chess of top quality, and the draw was a just result . Given that the Indian was playing with black pieces and that he had gone into the match as the less favoured of the two, Gukesh could be a little happier with the game than his Uzbek rival. The Chennai Grandmaster was in considerable time trouble on multiple occasions, but managed to solve his problems and found proper answers to the questions posed to him on the board by the confident Sindarov. The match has only begun, and there is plenty of chess left. It is a long match of 14 games, played in the classical time control, and the man who reaches 7.5 points will be the champion. The well-contested opening game would have given Gukesh, and his team comprising his coach and ‘seconds’, enough confidence, after several disappointing performances since he became the youngest World champion in history , at 18, by defeating China’s Ding Liren in Singapore two years ago. That match too had gone down the wire, with Gukesh winning the last of the 14 games, thanks to a terrible mistake towards the end by his rival.

Sindarov is just six months older than Gukesh, making the Geneva match the youngest in the 140-year-old history of the World championship: both players are 20. It is remarkable that Gukesh has already seen the highs and lows of life at such a young age. For his opponent, the last one year has been better than a dream: from World No. 26 he has risen to No. 4. Chess is getting younger. The next World championship could also very well have two young contenders. Grandmasters are usually said to peak when they are around 30 and chess is one game that even older players have continued to excel in. Viswanathan Anand was 48 when he won the World rapid chess championship . The match between Gukesh and Sindarov has attracted considerable interest from across the sporting world. After the 1972 match between Boris Spassky and Bobby Fischer — the defining moment of world chess — the World championship has earned a reputation as one of the planet’s most important sporting events. No battle between two of the world’s most talented men in chess has ever disappointed.

articles.title: Transfer assumption: On the SAD(B)-BJP alliance in Punjab
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: BJP and SAD(B) cannot count on their support bases adding up

Few parties understand the arithmetic of the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system, and the necessity for alliances in States where they are minor players, better than the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) . The BJP has never shied away from partnerships with little ideological cohesion if they keep it electorally relevant. India’s FPTP system is unforgiving to smaller parties in a crowded polity if their support base is limited and dispersed. Votes translate into seats only if the support crosses a certain threshold. In Punjab , the BJP, despite its best efforts, has remained confined to sections of urban Hindu voters. Even after years of poaching leaders from the perennially fractious Congress , and after polling nearly a fifth of the vote in the 2024 general election without winning a seat, it realises that it cannot be relevant without a partner with a wider rural base. The Shiromani Akali Dal (Badal) walked out of the BJP -led National Democratic Alliance in 2020 over the Centre’s farm laws, which were later repealed, as the farmers’ agitation threatened its base in rural Punjab. But much water has flowed down the many rivers of the northern State since then. The Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) has consolidated its hold in a crowded political space and is set to complete a full term. The Panthic vote, which used to be the SAD(B)’s core support base, has now fragmented. The SAD(B) appears to believe that it can regain ground only by expanding beyond its Panthic and rural constituencies, and that the farmers’ anger against the BJP is baggage from the past. It is this expedient calculation that now binds the two parties, despite six years of bitter attacks against each other. And it is also why the Union Home Minister, Amit Shah, has pointedly called the SAD(B) the “big brother” in Punjab after sealing the alliance.

The SAD(B)’s calculation may not work out as well as it hopes it would. Farmers’ anger against the BJP-led Centre has not entirely dissipated in rural Punjab. In earlier alliances, the two parties transferred votes to each other effectively, partly because their voters had fewer alternatives. But a revived Congress and an entrenched AAP have shown that they can win over urban Hindu voters wary of the Akalis and rural voters who are not inclined to back parties allied with the BJP. That these two sections will simply add up for the alliance is not certain. At best, the alliance consolidates enough of the anti-AAP vote to make this a clear three-cornered contest. Punjab is a sensitive border State and one of India’s granaries. It is also among India’s most indebted States, with a stagnating agrarian economy and a government that has expanded welfare expenditure despite strained finances. It needs a serious competition of ideas on what welfare it can afford and how to revive growth. The SAD(B)-BJP alliance , with its Panthic appeal on one side and Hindu consolidation on the other, instead offers a rehash of familiar identity politics. With AAP failing to deliver on governance, and the Congress stuck in its old ways, Punjab’s voters will have to decide who they dislike the least.

✍️ Editorial & Opinion 📅 28 Nov 2026 ⏱️ 4 Min Read

📰 Transfer assumption: On the SAD(B)-BJP alliance in Punjab

🎯 Exam Relevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
🔮 Futuristic Word Radar: Paragraph ke kisi bhi English word par Double-Click karein — turant uska Hinglish Meaning + Picture screen par dekhein!

BJP and SAD(B) cannot count on their support bases adding up

Few parties understand the arithmetic of the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system, and the necessity for alliances in States where they are minor players, better than the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) . The BJP has never shied away from partnerships with little ideological cohesion if they keep it electorally relevant. India’s FPTP system is unforgiving to smaller parties in a crowded polity if their support base is limited and dispersed. Votes translate into seats only if the support crosses a certain threshold. In Punjab , the BJP, despite its best efforts, has remained confined to sections of urban Hindu voters. Even after years of poaching leaders from the perennially fractious Congress , and after polling nearly a fifth of the vote in the 2024 general election without winning a seat, it realises that it cannot be relevant without a partner with a wider rural base. The Shiromani Akali Dal (Badal) walked out of the BJP -led National Democratic Alliance in 2020 over the Centre’s farm laws, which were later repealed, as the farmers’ agitation threatened its base in rural Punjab. But much water has flowed down the many rivers of the northern State since then. The Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) has consolidated its hold in a crowded political space and is set to complete a full term. The Panthic vote, which used to be the SAD(B)’s core support base, has now fragmented. The SAD(B) appears to believe that it can regain ground only by expanding beyond its Panthic and rural constituencies, and that the farmers’ anger against the BJP is baggage from the past. It is this expedient calculation that now binds the two parties, despite six years of bitter attacks against each other. And it is also why the Union Home Minister, Amit Shah, has pointedly called the SAD(B) the “big brother” in Punjab after sealing the alliance.

The SAD(B)’s calculation may not work out as well as it hopes it would. Farmers’ anger against the BJP-led Centre has not entirely dissipated in rural Punjab. In earlier alliances, the two parties transferred votes to each other effectively, partly because their voters had fewer alternatives. But a revived Congress and an entrenched AAP have shown that they can win over urban Hindu voters wary of the Akalis and rural voters who are not inclined to back parties allied with the BJP. That these two sections will simply add up for the alliance is not certain. At best, the alliance consolidates enough of the anti-AAP vote to make this a clear three-cornered contest. Punjab is a sensitive border State and one of India’s granaries. It is also among India’s most indebted States, with a stagnating agrarian economy and a government that has expanded welfare expenditure despite strained finances. It needs a serious competition of ideas on what welfare it can afford and how to revive growth. The SAD(B)-BJP alliance , with its Panthic appeal on one side and Hindu consolidation on the other, instead offers a rehash of familiar identity politics. With AAP failing to deliver on governance, and the Congress stuck in its old ways, Punjab’s voters will have to decide who they dislike the least.

articles.title: Global fashion brands shift orders from Bangladesh to India amid unrest
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Between November 1 and 18, brands diverted about $254 million worth ⁠of orders from Bangladesh, with most moving to neighbouring India, the owners said

Global fashion retailers including Zara and H&M shifted nearly a tenth of their monthly orders from ‌Bangladesh to other Asian manufacturing hubs in the first half of November, as labour unrest disrupted production and rising ​costs eroded the country’s competitive edge, three factory owners said.

Between November 1 and 18, brands diverted about $254 million worth ⁠of orders from Bangladesh, with most moving to neighbouring India, the owners said, a shift that represents a major blow to a key pillar of Bangladesh’s economy and could extend beyond the current unrest.

Industry leaders have said rising wages, energy shortages and political uncertainty have weakened the low-cost advantage that helped ‌make Bangladesh the world’s second apparel exporter after China, prompting global brands to diversify sourcing.

The protests have caused more than $400 million in production losses, according to the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA), in an industry that accounts for more ‌than 80% of Bangladesh’s export earnings and nearly 40% of its manufacturing jobs.
India has emerged ‌as ⁠the biggest beneficiary, while buyers are also looking to Vietnam, Cambodia and Indonesia to reduce supply-chain risks and improve delivery ⁠reliability, industry leaders said.
Those pressures intensified on Wednesday when Bangladesh approved a 36% increase in the minimum wage for garment workers, the smallest rise in four decades.

The increase fell well short of workers’ demands to more than double wages, triggering fresh clashes with police even as Abdur Rahman Tarafder, secretary of the Ministry of Labour and Employment, ​said the wage increase was “satisfactory” and that he hoped all ‌workers would resume work from Saturday.
Industry leaders said the increase would nevertheless narrow Bangladesh’s labour-cost advantage over India, although union groups argue the wages remain low by global industry standards.
Babul Akhter, a union leader and workers’ representative on the government-appointed wage board, said brands should not use the unrest to justify shifting orders out of Bangladesh.

He said retailers already factor political instability and labour ‌unrest into sourcing decisions, making such moves “hard to justify” and raising “serious doubts” whether the unrest was more than an excuse.

articles.title: Kumari Sachu honoured withcultural excellence award

fullParagraphs: Veteran actress, comedian and dancer Kumari Sachu was honoured with the Dr. Mrs. YGP Award of Cultural Excellence at a ceremony hosted by Bharat Kalachar at Rama Rao Kala Mantap, Karnataka Sangha School in T. Nagar in the city on Friday.
Instituted in the name of the late Smt. Kalyani Venkataraman to mark the 101st birth anniversary celebrations of Dr. Mrs. YGP, the award was presented by Rtn. Ravi Venkataraman.

The event was graced by veteran actor Sivakumar as the chief guest and Rtn. Shriram Duvvuri, District Governor, Rotary International District 3233, as the guest of honour. Mr. Sivakumar and Kalaimamani Bombay Gnanam, renowned theatre and film writer, director, and producer, felicitated the awardee during the ceremony.

Political & National Report: Kumari Sachu honoured withcultural excellence award. This development is a key milestone in India's ongoing legislative, judicial, and constitutional governance framework.

articles.title: Karnataka government serves show-cause notice to IOCL terminal in Bengaluru over ethanol measurement discrepancies
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The action follows inspections initiated by the Department of Legal Metrology, Karnataka, at the terminals of oil marketing companies, taking the checks of fuel samples for ethanol blend one step further

The Karnataka government on Friday served a show-cause notice on Indian Oil Corporation Limited (IOCL) over discrepancies in the measurement of ethanol and motor gasoline at its terminal in Devanagonthi, Bengaluru, and directed the oil marketing company (OMC) to submit an explanation within seven days.
The action follows inspections initiated by the Department of Legal Metrology, Karnataka, at the terminals of oil marketing companies.

Tests of samples from petrol stations in Karnataka by the State government had revealed ethanol blending to be as high as 32% in some cases, Food, Civil Supplies, Consumer Affairs and Legal Metrology Minister Rizwan Arshad claimed earlier this month. This was denied by OMCs and Union Ministers.
Mr. Arshad had also written to the Union government seeking display of accurate ethanol blending in petrol at every station.

According to the show-cause notice, officials detected discrepancies in the quantities of ethanol and motor gasoline dispensed through mass flow meters during an inspection at the IOCL terminal on Wednesday (November 25).

According to the Minister, the inspection was conducted using the “master proving” test method. At Bay No. 9, officials found that the meter was dispensing 14 litres of ethanol in excess for every 3,000 litres. At the same bay, the quantity of motor gasoline supplied was found to be 4 to 6 litres short for every 3,000 litres. Another mass flow meter at Bay No. 4 was also found to be dispensing an additional three litres of ethanol for every 3,000 litres, the notice stated.

Mr. Arshad said that the discrepancies exceeded the permissible limits prescribed under the Legal Metrology Act, 2009, and the rules framed under it. “The inaccuracies in measurement could adversely affect the interests of consumers, distributors and other stakeholders dealing with petroleum products,” he said.

The show-cause notice, issued to the Deputy General Manager in charge of the Devanagonthi terminal, has sought a written explanation within seven days of its receipt, warning that failure to submit a satisfactory explanation within the stipulated period could lead to further legal and departmental action against the terminal and the officials responsible.

The department has asked IOCL to explain the reasons behind the discrepancies and provide details of the measures taken to ensure the accuracy of the mass flow meters and associated batch control units. It has also sought records of their latest calibration and maintenance, along with details of corrective measures proposed to address the discrepancies.
Further, the department has directed IOCL not to use the affected measurement systems for commercial transactions until their accuracy and compliance with prescribed legal standards are verified.

articles.title: Civil society groups urge Karnataka Chief Minister to scrutinise SIR deletions ahead of local polls
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Members of various civil society groups under the banner of the “Anti-SIR alliance” on Friday submitted a memorandum to Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar, demanding that the State government reject the final electoral roll published after the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and take a clear stand against the exercise, with local body elections approaching.

The alliance said the final electoral roll was riddled with errors and demanded that the 2025 electoral roll be restored, subjected to public scrutiny and revised in a voter-friendly manner before being used for local body elections.

The alliance also cited the Election Commission’s recent instructions to States conducting SIR to “revisit deleted and left-out voters”, publish booth-wise deletion lists and make efforts to restore those wrongly excluded. It said these directions pointed to serious shortcomings in the SIR.

The groups, in their letter, also criticised statements by some Congress Ministers that Karnataka had not lost anything through SIR and could use the revised rolls for local body elections. The alliance said the government should not assess the exercise through the narrow lens of electoral gains or losses. It also pressed for a social audit to establish the legitimacy of deletions made during SIR.

articles.title: RBI cuts daily CRR maintenance to 90%, to unlock over ₹40,000 crore
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The latest relaxation is expected to improve banks’ liquidity flexibility and support credit deployment.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Friday eased the minimum daily maintenance requirement for the cash reserve ratio (CRR) from 99% to 90%, a move expected to release more than ₹40,000 crore into the banking system and provide banks with additional funds for lending.

“On the basis of an assessment of the current and evolving macroeconomic situation and liquidity conditions, it has been decided to reduce the minimum daily maintenance of the cash reserve ratio (CRR) from 99% of the requirement to 90% effective from the fortnight beginning December 1, 2026,” the RBI said.

Under the revised arrangement, scheduled banks will be required to maintain at least 90% of their prescribed CRR on each day of the reporting fortnight. However, the average daily CRR maintained during the fortnight must not fall below the level prescribed by the RBI.

With the prescribed CRR currently at 3% of a bank’s net demand and time liabilities (NDTL), banks will now have greater flexibility in managing their daily cash balances, while continuing to meet the overall fortnightly requirement.

The latest move reverses the tightening introduced on October 9, shortly after the previous Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting. At the time, the RBI had raised the minimum daily CRR maintenance requirement from 90% to 99%, effective from the fortnight beginning October 16, 2026.
The earlier move came when the banking system was flush with liquidity following substantial mobilisation of funds through foreign currency non-resident (FCNR-B) deposits.

The latest move reverses the tightening introduced on October 9, shortly after the previous Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting. At the time, the RBI had raised the minimum daily CRR maintenance requirement from 90% to 99%, effective from the fortnight beginning October 16, 2026.

The earlier move came when the banking system was flush with liquidity following substantial mobilisation of funds through foreign currency non-resident (FCNR-B) deposits.

articles.title: The fiscal cost of cash-transfer schemes
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: A social policy is often based on expected electoral gain, and is implemented without any ex ante appraisal; since cash transfers and subsidies are perpetual in nature and politically hard to reverse, such continuous commitment of financial resources demands prior evaluation and real-time monitoring to address potential shortcomings

Business Standard reported on May 13, 2026 that “Cash-transfer promises have moved from the margins of Indian election manifestos to the centre of political competition, with parties across States promising monthly or one-time payments.” Quoting a PRS Legislative Research report, it further said, “12 States are expected to spend nearly ₹1.68 trillion on unconditional cash-transfer schemes for women in 2025-26, … the outgo is roughly equivalent to 0.5 per cent of India’s GDP, compared with less than 0.2 per cent two years ago.”

The RBI report ‘State Finance: Study of State Budgets 2025-26’ reported that the total subsidy outlay increased from ₹1.87 trillion in 2018-19 to ₹4.26 trillion in 2025-26. States often implement promises from their election manifestos soon after forming the government and just before the next election, without any serious assessment of needs or financial commitments.

Conception and funding of an infrastructure project are guided by a Detailed Project Report (DPR) that specifies objectives, alternatives considered, financial and economic analysis, risk mitigation, baseline data, and success criteria. A social policy, by contrast, is often the outcome of an electoral promise or based on expected electoral gain, and is implemented without any comparable ex ante appraisal. Social policies affect human capabilities more directly than infrastructure projects.

The scarcity of public resources and their alternative uses make ex ante appraisal of social sector schemes essential. Moreover, social policies are vulnerable to electoral clientelism, and should therefore adhere to the same principles of public expenditure as infrastructure projects — evidence, accountability, equity, efficiency and fiscal responsibility as infrastructure. The claim that the benefits of social policies are not quantifiable should not stop ex ante appraisal, as methodologies exist to overcome this barrier.

An ex ante appraisal of a social project leaves an audit trail: the legislature, auditors, the media, and citizens can ask whether the project delivered what it promised. Many social schemes are implemented without the assessment of needs, identification of potential beneficiaries, or adequate funding, and a bureaucratic, top-down, target-chasing approach often replaces a democratic, bottom-up planning and implementation process.
This article explores the fiscal and economic fallout of cash transfers and universal subsidies.

If politics decides the desired social ends of such schemes, public finance and administration should decide the programme’s funding priority, the quantum of funding and the implementation process required to achieve those ends.

Prioritising expenditure is the first step in checking the desirability of public expenditure. For example, the Government of Tamil Nadu allocated nearly ₹1,000 crore in 2026-27 to provide scholarships for girls and boys from Government schools to continue higher education. A recent report in a Tamil Magazine ( Ananda Vikatan , November 18, 2026), based on replies it received to RTI applications, found 7,198 vacancies in permanent teaching positions in Government Arts and Science Colleges. If we include teacher vacancies in professional colleges and universities, the number should be nearly 9,000. Filling these vacancies, delayed for over a decade, would cost ₹1,080 crore per annum, rising every year thereafter. With a huge revenue deficit and fiscal deficit, the State budget lacks the revenue cushion to spend an additional ₹1,080 crore per annum. Prioritising is a normative decision: filling vacancies ensures students learn from regular teachers, whereas funding scholarships alone sends them to colleges without regular teachers.

Deciding the quantum of funding and the process of execution requires ex ante evaluation. This should be explicitly oriented toward designing programmes that maximise impact for a given cost, using behavioural models and micro-simulations to predict the effects of hypothetical programmes before implementation.

For instance, a universal subsidy scheme is a trade-off between inclusion and exclusion errors. If it is truly universal, the scheme commits the error of including the undeserving and thus reduces the per-capita benefit to people in need. In a target-oriented scheme, it commits the error of excluding the deserving, but it increases the per-capita benefit to people in need. The choice between the two requires ex ante appraisal of such schemes.

articles.title: Experts say new U.S. tariffs do not pose substantial threat, India should not rush into trade deal
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The latest proposal by the USTR takes the tariff framework on India back to what it was at the start of trade deal negotiations

The new 25% tariffs proposed by the U.S. on India do not pose a substantial risk to Indian exports, and India should go ahead with a trade deal only if it is balanced and reciprocal, according to exporters and trade and tariff experts.

An analysis of India’s trade relationship with the U.S. over the last two years showed that the latest tariffs announced by the U.S. have returned the tariff relationship to where it was at the start of trade deal negotiations.
The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative on Wednesday proposed a net tariff of 25% on goods imported from India, which could be reduced to 17% if a trade deal is signed by the two countries.

The proposed 25% tariff is nearly the same as the 26% tariff U.S. President Donald Trump had originally proposed in his ‘Liberation Day’ reciprocal tariff measure in April 2025. A week later, Mr. Trump paused these tariffs in a bid to secure trade deals with other countries.

In July 2025, he announced a 25% tariff on India, the same as what the USTR is now proposing. But Mr. Trump soon announced an additional 25% tariff as a penalty for India’s Russian oil imports taking the total tariff on Indian goods to 50%.

During that time, Mr. Trump also announced a 50% tariff on the import of steel and aluminium from all countries. The latest tariffs by the USTR are not in addition to those tariffs, meaning Indian steel and aluminium will continue to attract a 50% duty.

In February 2026, India and the U.S. issued a joint statement announcing the framework for an interim deal on trade, under which the U.S. would reduce its tariffs on Indian goods to 18%. This is very close to the 17% the U.S. is proposing now, should a deal be signed, nearly 10 months after the joint statement was issued.
As such, the pre-deal, post-deal, and steel and aluminium tariffs by the U.S. on India largely remain where they were at the start of negotiations.
Exporters and trade experts have said that India should proceed with a trade deal only if it satisfies Indian interests.

“FIEO supports the government’s efforts to conclude the Bilateral Trade Agreement at an early date,” said S.C. Ralhan, president of the Federation of Indian Export Organisations. “The agreement should be balanced and reciprocal, safeguard India’s long-term economic and developmental interests, and ensure that Indian exporters can compete on a level-playing field with suppliers from other countries in the U.S. market.”

articles.title: Net FDI fell to more than 5.5-year low in September 2026, as outflows jumped 40%
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: Despite September’s performance, net FDI in the first half of the financial year was more than 20% higher than in the same period last year

Net foreign direct investment (FDI) into India in September 2026 fell to its lowest level in at least 5.5 years, with outflows exceeding inflows by nearly $5 billion, data released by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) shows.

This was driven by a simultaneous slump in gross inflows and a jump in outflows. However, net FDI in the first half of the financial year (April-September 2026) was more than 20% higher than in the same period of the previous year.
September’s net FDI figure of -$4.95 billion was the lowest since at least March 2021, the earliest month for which data is accessible.

Direct investment refers to the inflows that give the investor substantial control over an asset or means of production, as opposed to portfolio investments, which are typically more in the nature of speculative purchases of minor shareholding.
Gross inflows, or the total amount of direct investment entering the country, fell to $5.9 billion in September 2026, 46.6% lower than in August, and 17.6% lower than in September of last year.

According to the RBI, around two-thirds of the gross inflows were channelled into manufacturing, communication, and computer services sectors, with Singapore and the U.S. as the major source countries.

Total outflows climbed to $10.8 billion in September 2026, nearly 40% higher than in August, and 15% higher than in September last year. Within this, repatriation of profits by foreign companies in India grew to $6.4 billion, nearly 37% higher than in the same month last year, and the highest since at least March 2021.
Outward investments made by Indian companies grew to a five-month high of $4.4 billion in September 2026.

The RBI says that of the outward investments, manufacturing, and financial, insurance and business services sectors accounted for about four-fifths of the amount that flowed out of India, with The Netherlands, Singapore and the U.S. serving as the major destinations.

The U.S. military said on Friday (November 27, 2026) ‌it disabled a commercial ship on Thursday (November 26, 2026) ​after it attempted to ⁠run the US blockade of Iran, while an adviser to the Iranian supreme leader ‌said Iran would keep the Strait of Hormuz shut ‌while vowing to break the embargo.

CENTCOM disabled a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman, Nov. 26, after the crew attempted to run the U.S. naval blockade, despite multiple warnings, following departure from Bandar Abbas. A U.S. military aircraft launched precision munitions that struck the stern of Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer. The ship's propulsion was ultimately disabled and the civilian crew was unharmed. articles.title: Chinese Military tests new Taiwan landing tactics in coastal drills
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The exercise in Dacheng Bay was first spotted on November 1, according to a report by geospatial data company ingeniSPACE reviewed by Reuters

China is staging a weeks-long amphibious landing drill in the province facing Taiwan, testing a new method to land troops ashore by linking civilian vessels ‌into a makeshift floating bridge, satellite images and a research report showed.

China views democratically governed Taiwan as ​its own territory, despite Taipei's rejection of Beijing's sovereignty claims, and has never renounced the use of force to ⁠bring it under Chinese control.

The exercise, in Dacheng Bay in China's southeastern province of Fujian, was first spotted on November 1, according to satellite images and a report by geospatial data company ingeniSPACE reviewed by Reuters.

"The People's Liberation Army appeared to be rehearsing low-signature methods to provide logistical support ‌to forces that could be involved in a first island chain invasion scenario," said Jason Wang, the company's chief operating officer.
"Using civilian ships to enable bridging of heavy equipment and materiel from deeper waters creates additional locations they can use ‌along the Taiwan coastline."

A senior security official briefed on the drill in Dacheng Bay, just 280 km (175 miles) from ‌Taiwan's ⁠main island, confirmed it was still in progress on Friday, but made no direct link to local elections ⁠set for the next day.

Analysis of the images from November 1 to 16 showed the vessels manoeuvred around the bay, forming and dismantling a floating bridge about 800 m (2,600 ft) long, in activity also seen in images from commercial providers Vantor and Planet Labs.

Eight civilian vessels participated, made up ​of four barges, two semi-submersible and two powered, along with ‌four landing craft, as well as smaller support vessels and Chinese navy ships nearby, ingeniSPACE's analysis and tracking data showed.

No purpose-built bridging equipment was observed, suggesting China's military may be honing its use of existing civilian maritime resources to improvise landing infrastructure in a combat scenario, ingeniSPACE said.
The senior security official confirmed the report details.

Since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, several countries bordering the conflict have reported incursions or drone and missile crashes on their territory.

"Fighter jets from NATO's air-policing mission in the Baltic States were scrambled, and an interceptor drone from the national armed forces was deployed," it said, without specifying the origin of the drone.

articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The intrusion at Cloud One was discovered within the past month or so ⁠during work to upgrade the system, two people familiar with the matter said

Hackers have breached the U.S. Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform, three people familiar with ‌the matter told Reuters , in a development that could jeopardize a vast swathe of sensitive tactical, ​personnel and logistics data.

The intrusion at Cloud One was discovered within the past month or so ⁠during work to upgrade the system, two of the people said, adding that the discovery has led to disruption across the platform. Reuters could not establish the identity of the hackers, the full scope of the intrusion or whether any data had been stolen.

In ‌a statement to Reuters , the Air Force said it "does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems. We continuously take prudent measures to protect Department (of the ‌Air Force) information, systems and mission capabilities."

Initiated in 2017, Cloud One was meant to serve ‌as ⁠a one-stop shop for the Air Force's IT needs, combining the resources of four operators — Microsoft, Amazon, ⁠Oracle and Alphabet — to power scores of applications including ones that manage personnel data and pay or logistics and maintenance.

Among them are the Air Force's Cloud-Based Command and Control, which collates air defence radar and other data feeds from across North America, and the Theater Integrated Combat Munitions ​System, which tracks bombs and missiles across more than ‌200 U.S. Air Force locations around the world.
SAIC was the prime contractor for Cloud One until 2025, when Leidos took over. SAIC did not respond to a request seeking comment. Leidos referred questions to the Air Force.
Cloud One is among the U.S. military's biggest cloud platforms, according to two of the sources.

articles.title: Hyderabad’s air pollution puts focus on hospitals; doctors call for city-level health database
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Hospitals want to share anonymised data on respiratory illnesses, strokes and cardiovascular conditions, while doctors propose using daily AQI readings to alert vulnerable patients

With Hyderabad recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) of over 300 on Deepavali and many other days recording poor air quality earlier this year, doctors and public health experts have called for a coordinated effort by hospitals to track the health effects of pollution and build a city-level database that can help shape public policy.

The issue came into focus during a panel discussion on ‘Impact of Mobility on Air Quality and Public Health’ at Cyberabad Moves, where doctors said that the effects of polluted air went beyond respiratory illnesses and were also linked to cardiovascular problems and strokes. They stressed that the health consequences of daily exposure to pollution, particularly during commutes, needed to be documented through local medical data.

Pawan Mukulutla of WRI India, who moderated the discussion, pointed out that congestion was only the most visible consequence of the way people travelled. The less visible costs included exposure to polluted air, unsafe roads and the lack of pedestrian infrastructure. He cited Hyderabad’s AQI crossing 300 on Deepavali and said particulate matter levels, including PM2.5 and PM10, had been several times above prescribed thresholds.

Dr. Sudheer Vinnamala, Regional Medical Director of KIMS, said hospitals could work together to create a Hyderabad-level health database by sharing anonymised information on respiratory illnesses, strokes and cardiovascular conditions with public health authorities.

“What you can’t measure, you can’t manage,” he said, arguing that such a database could help identify vulnerable groups and establish a clearer picture of the relationship between air quality and health outcomes.

He said doctors could also use daily AQI information to alert patients with asthma and other respiratory conditions when pollution levels deteriorated, allowing them to take precautions and avoid unnecessary exposure. Hospitals could play a role in reducing pollution and traffic by encouraging carpooling, staggering appointments and arranging last-mile transport links from Metro stations.

Dr Vishwanath Gella, a pulmonologist at AIG Hospitals, said pollution affected people with and without pre-existing health conditions. He said doctors were seeing patients with asthma, respiratory infections and other lung-related complaints, with an increase in cases during periods of poor air quality, particularly around Deepavali and in winter.

Dr Shailaja Tetali of the Public Health Foundation of India said research into school travel patterns showed that around 80 per cent of children lived within two to three kilometres of their schools. A majority travelled by public transport, walked or cycled.

While walking and cycling offered physical activity, children using these modes were also exposed to roadside pollution and faced road safety risks. She said improving infrastructure around schools could address several of these concerns, as interventions within a three-kilometre radius could cover a large proportion of children’s daily journeys.

She called for authorities to act on existing evidence instead of repeatedly commissioning studies, suggesting that interventions could first be tested in smaller areas and then replicated across the city.

fullParagraphs: The webinar discussed the role of robotics in improving surgical precision, implant positioning and recovery in total knee replacement

The Hindu , in association with Kauvery Hospital, conducted a webinar on Friday titled ‘The Role of Robotics in Knee Replacement’. Orthopaedic specialists discussed the use of robotic-assisted technology in total knee replacement (TKR), its benefits, post-operative recovery, costs and the role of surgeons in performing the procedure.

The experts were Mukunth K., senior consultant, orthopaedic surgeon, joint replacement and sports injuries, Kauvery Hospital, Alwarpet; P.R. Ramasamy, head of the department of orthopaedics and pelviacetabular and joint replacement surgeon, Kauvery Hospital, Tiruchi; and Manivannan, consultant, orthopaedics, arthroscopy and joint replacement surgeon, Kauvery Hospital, Salem.

Dr. Mukunth explained how robotic-assisted technology helps surgeons plan knee replacement procedures through bone mapping, precise measurements and real-time guidance. He said the technology helped surgeons make accurate bone cuts and position implants closer to the intended alignment. He compared the robot’s role to GPS navigation, emphasising that the surgeon remained in control of the procedure.

He said manual measurements during conventional surgery could vary by 2–3 mm, even in experienced hands. Greater precision in bone cuts and implant alignment could help reduce soft-tissue trauma and blood loss during surgery and improve post-operative outcomes.

Dr. Ramasamy explained the steps involved in robotic-assisted knee replacement. He said the procedure involved less damage to the surrounding bone, which could make a future revision surgery easier. He also clarified that robotic technology was not used for revision surgery in patients who had undergone conventional knee replacement 15–20 years earlier. The aim of robotic-assisted TKR was not limited to pain relief but also included helping patients return to their routine activities sooner, he said.

Dr. Manivannan discussed post-operative recovery and mobility. He said accurate implant positioning could help patients regain mobility and muscle strength sooner, with recovery potentially being two to three weeks faster than with conventional surgery. Hospital stays could also be shorter, and patients could become fully functional within six to eight weeks.

Responding to questions on cost, the panel said robotic-assisted knee replacement costs between ₹3.5 lakh and ₹5.5 lakh, depending on the hospital, city and patient’s health condition and that the procedure is covered under health insurance.

articles.title: COP31: India welcomes $50 million climate fund pledge, says adaptation needs far greater
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: India has welcomed a $50 million pledge to the Adaptation Fund at the UN climate change conference COP31 , but said the contribution was inadequate given the scale of adaptation needs in developing countries and stressed that financial pledges must translate into timely and accessible resources.

In a written interview with PTI , Union Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav said the removal of the $120 billion adaptation finance figure from the proposed cover text, and the failure to reach an overarching agreement at COP31, were disappointing.

“The absence of an agreed formulation on the $120 billion adaptation finance figure in the final outcome is disappointing. It reflects the continuing difficulties in securing predictable financial commitments and agreement on how progress towards the existing goal of tripling adaptation finance by 2035 should be measured and monitored,” he said.

Mr. Yadav, however, noted that the absence of a cover decision did not extinguish developed countries’ commitments under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and the Paris Agreement.

He said adaptation was not a secondary consideration but an immediate developmental necessity for millions of vulnerable people. India had consistently maintained that adaptation finance must be adequate, predictable, primarily public and substantially grant-based, he added.

“Developing countries should not be compelled to incur additional debt to protect vulnerable communities from climate impacts. At COP31, India worked closely with Like-Minded Developing Countries (LMDC) and G77 (largest bloc of 134 developing nations plus China) partners to seek stronger outcomes on adaptation finance and implementation support,” Yadav said.

He said India would continue to push for enhanced financial support, transparency in delivery and implementation of existing commitments, particularly for the poorest and most climate-vulnerable countries.

Mr. Yadav said that the failure to reach consensus on the proposed overarching agreement, the Antalya Pact, should not overshadow progress made on other issues and that the nation continues to deliver substantial climate action through its domestic efforts and resources.

“India engaged constructively throughout the Conference, working closely with BASIC, Like-Minded Developing Countries (LMDCs) and G77 to secure a balanced and equitable outcome. We regret that consensus on the proposed Antalya Pact could not be reached. However, this should not overshadow the substantive progress achieved on several important issues,” he said.

On procedural decisions at COP31, Mr. Yadav said the Climate Finance Work Programme decision had established a process for further discussions, while the outcome on the Just Transition Work Programme was more substantive.

articles.title: Bombay High Court puts road project on hold till State files report on mangrove loss, compensatory measures
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The Bombay High Court directed the State to submit figures documenting tree cover, losses, and five-year survival rates before any orders are passed

The Bombay High Court has withheld permission for a road project in Mumbai until the State government submits a detailed report on measures taken to compensate for the loss of mangroves. The court also stated that ‘afforestation’ efforts must be completed before seeking clearances and that the process should not be treated as a mere formality.

A Bench comprising Chief Justice Mahesh C. Tripathi and Justice Advait Sethna made these remarks while hearing a plea by the Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority (MMRDA) seeking permission to divert 0.2869 hectares of mangrove land in the Bandra-Kurla Complex area to construct an Automated Rapid Transit System covering 8.85 km.

A 2018 High Court ruling mandated court approval for developments affecting wetlands. Though the project will not require clearing mangroves, it impacts six trees, necessitating the planting of 100 trees as compensation.

Advocate Saket Mone, representing the MMRDA, argued that the Automated Rapid Transit System fulfills key connectivity needs. He added that tree planting falls under the jurisdiction of the Forest Department. In response, the Bench questioned why officials had not initiated remedial action when conceptualising the project.

Advocate General of Maharashtra Milind Sathe attributed the planting delays to a shortage of saline land, noting that saplings must be planted before the monsoon to ensure survival. However, the Bench pointed out a gap between regulators’ filings and ground reality, questioning how authorities could grant permission when rules mandate 30% tree cover.

The Court directed the State to submit figures documenting tree cover, losses, and five-year survival rates before any orders are passed. Stating that it does not oppose the project but will not proceed without full compliance, the Court posted the matter to November 30.
Mr. Mone was briefed by advocate Fatema Ansari, while Mr. Sathe was briefed by Government Pleader Onkar Chandurkar.

🚀 Science, Tech & Environment 📅 27 Nov 2026 ⏱️ 2 Min Read

🎯 Exam Relevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
🔮 Futuristic Word Radar: Paragraph ke kisi bhi English word par Double-Click karein — turant uska Hinglish Meaning + Picture screen par dekhein!

The Bombay High Court directed the State to submit figures documenting tree cover, losses, and five-year survival rates before any orders are passed

The Bombay High Court has withheld permission for a road project in Mumbai until the State government submits a detailed report on measures taken to compensate for the loss of mangroves. The court also stated that ‘afforestation’ efforts must be completed before seeking clearances and that the process should not be treated as a mere formality.

A Bench comprising Chief Justice Mahesh C. Tripathi and Justice Advait Sethna made these remarks while hearing a plea by the Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority (MMRDA) seeking permission to divert 0.2869 hectares of mangrove land in the Bandra-Kurla Complex area to construct an Automated Rapid Transit System covering 8.85 km.

A 2018 High Court ruling mandated court approval for developments affecting wetlands. Though the project will not require clearing mangroves, it impacts six trees, necessitating the planting of 100 trees as compensation.

Advocate Saket Mone, representing the MMRDA, argued that the Automated Rapid Transit System fulfills key connectivity needs. He added that tree planting falls under the jurisdiction of the Forest Department. In response, the Bench questioned why officials had not initiated remedial action when conceptualising the project.

Advocate General of Maharashtra Milind Sathe attributed the planting delays to a shortage of saline land, noting that saplings must be planted before the monsoon to ensure survival. However, the Bench pointed out a gap between regulators’ filings and ground reality, questioning how authorities could grant permission when rules mandate 30% tree cover.

The Court directed the State to submit figures documenting tree cover, losses, and five-year survival rates before any orders are passed. Stating that it does not oppose the project but will not proceed without full compliance, the Court posted the matter to November 30.

Mr. Mone was briefed by advocate Fatema Ansari, while Mr. Sathe was briefed by Government Pleader Onkar Chandurkar.

articles.title: MGM Healthcare Malar launches AI-powered MRI facility in Chennai
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: According to the hospital, the technology can reduce scan time; a brain MRI that conventionally takes about 35 minutes can now be completed in under 14 minutes
MGM Healthcare Malar, Adyar, has launched an AI-powered MRI facility, offering specialised imaging services for neurological, cardiac, musculoskeletal, spinal, and other conditions.
The facility was inaugurated by J. Radhakrishnan, Chairperson of the Tamil Nadu Electricity Regulatory Commission, on Thursday (November 26, 2026).

The system uses deep learning algorithms to correct motion-related artefacts and improve image quality, potentially reducing the need for repeat scans. It also offers specialised fetal and breast MRI, cardiac MRI, whole-body imaging, diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), and perfusion imaging.

According to the hospital, the technology can also reduce scan time. A brain MRI that conventionally takes about 35 minutes can now be completed in under 14 minutes. This could benefit patients who find it difficult to remain still for prolonged periods due to pain or discomfort.

Thinesh Ram, senior consultant and head of Imaging and Interventional Radiology, MGM Healthcare Malar, said the system would enable more detailed evaluation of neural pathways and expand the range of diagnostic assessments.

S. Kripanandh, chief operating officer, MGM Healthcare Malar, Adyar, and group chief business officer, said the facility would strengthen the hospital’s diagnostic capabilities and expand access to advanced imaging services in the neighbourhood.

articles.title: Transfer assumption: On the SAD(B)-BJP alliance in Punjab
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: BJP and SAD(B) cannot count on their support bases adding up

Few parties understand the arithmetic of the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system, and the necessity for alliances in States where they are minor players, better than the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) . The BJP has never shied away from partnerships with little ideological cohesion if they keep it electorally relevant. India’s FPTP system is unforgiving to smaller parties in a crowded polity if their support base is limited and dispersed. Votes translate into seats only if the support crosses a certain threshold. In Punjab , the BJP, despite its best efforts, has remained confined to sections of urban Hindu voters. Even after years of poaching leaders from the perennially fractious Congress , and after polling nearly a fifth of the vote in the 2024 general election without winning a seat, it realises that it cannot be relevant without a partner with a wider rural base. The Shiromani Akali Dal (Badal) walked out of the BJP -led National Democratic Alliance in 2020 over the Centre’s farm laws, which were later repealed, as the farmers’ agitation threatened its base in rural Punjab. But much water has flowed down the many rivers of the northern State since then. The Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) has consolidated its hold in a crowded political space and is set to complete a full term. The Panthic vote, which used to be the SAD(B)’s core support base, has now fragmented. The SAD(B) appears to believe that it can regain ground only by expanding beyond its Panthic and rural constituencies, and that the farmers’ anger against the BJP is baggage from the past. It is this expedient calculation that now binds the two parties, despite six years of bitter attacks against each other. And it is also why the Union Home Minister, Amit Shah, has pointedly called the SAD(B) the “big brother” in Punjab after sealing the alliance.

The SAD(B)’s calculation may not work out as well as it hopes it would. Farmers’ anger against the BJP-led Centre has not entirely dissipated in rural Punjab. In earlier alliances, the two parties transferred votes to each other effectively, partly because their voters had fewer alternatives. But a revived Congress and an entrenched AAP have shown that they can win over urban Hindu voters wary of the Akalis and rural voters who are not inclined to back parties allied with the BJP. That these two sections will simply add up for the alliance is not certain. At best, the alliance consolidates enough of the anti-AAP vote to make this a clear three-cornered contest. Punjab is a sensitive border State and one of India’s granaries. It is also among India’s most indebted States, with a stagnating agrarian economy and a government that has expanded welfare expenditure despite strained finances. It needs a serious competition of ideas on what welfare it can afford and how to revive growth. The SAD(B)-BJP alliance , with its Panthic appeal on one side and Hindu consolidation on the other, instead offers a rehash of familiar identity politics. With AAP failing to deliver on governance, and the Congress stuck in its old ways, Punjab’s voters will have to decide who they dislike the least.

articles.summary: BJP and SAD(B) cannot count on their support bases adding up
articles.keyPoints:
• BJP and SAD(B) cannot count on their support bases adding up
• Few parties understand the arithmetic of the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system, and the necessity for alliances in States where they are minor players, better than the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) . The BJP has never shied away from partnerships with little ideological cohesion if they keep it electorally relevant. India’s FPTP system is unforgiving to smaller parties in a crowded polity if their support base is limited and dispersed. Votes translate into seats only if the support crosses a certain threshold. In Punjab , the BJP, despite its best efforts, has remained confined to sections of urban Hindu voters. Even after years of poaching leaders from the perennially fractious Congress , and after polling nearly a fifth of the vote in the 2024 general election without winning a seat, it realises that it cannot be relevant without a partner with a wider rural base. The Shiromani Akali Dal (Badal) walked out of the BJP -led National Democratic Alliance in 2020 over the Centre’s farm laws, which were later repealed, as the farmers’ agitation threatened its base in rural Punjab. But much water has flowed down the many rivers of the northern State since then. The Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) has consolidated its hold in a crowded political space and is set to complete a full term. The Panthic vote, which used to be the SAD(B)’s core support base, has now fragmented. The SAD(B) appears to believe that it can regain ground only by expanding beyond its Panthic and rural constituencies, and that the farmers’ anger against the BJP is baggage from the past. It is this expedient calculation that now binds the two parties, despite six years of bitter attacks against each other. And it is also why the Union Home Minister, Amit Shah, has pointedly called the SAD(B) the “big brother” in Punjab after sealing the alliance.
• The SAD(B)’s calculation may not work out as well as it hopes it would. Farmers’ anger against the BJP-led Centre has not entirely dissipated in rural Punjab. In earlier alliances, the two parties transferred votes to each other effectively, partly because their voters had fewer alternatives. But a revived Congress and an entrenched AAP have shown that they can win over urban Hindu voters wary of the Akalis and rural voters who are not inclined to back parties allied with the BJP. That these two sections will simply add up for the alliance is not certain. At best, the alliance consolidates enough of the anti-AAP vote to make this a clear three-cornered contest. Punjab is a sensitive border State and one of India’s granaries. It is also among India’s most indebted States, with a stagnating agrarian economy and a government that has expanded welfare expenditure despite strained finances. It needs a serious competition of ideas on what welfare it can afford and how to revive growth. The SAD(B)-BJP alliance , with its Panthic appeal on one side and Hindu consolidation on the other, instead offers a rehash of familiar identity politics. With AAP failing to deliver on governance, and the Congress stuck in its old ways, Punjab’s voters will have to decide who they dislike the least.

articles.title: Global fashion brands shift orders from Bangladesh to India amid unrest
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Between November 1 and 18, brands diverted about $254 million worth ⁠of orders from Bangladesh, with most moving to neighbouring India, the owners said

Global fashion retailers including Zara and H&M shifted nearly a tenth of their monthly orders from ‌Bangladesh to other Asian manufacturing hubs in the first half of November, as labour unrest disrupted production and rising ​costs eroded the country’s competitive edge, three factory owners said.

Between November 1 and 18, brands diverted about $254 million worth ⁠of orders from Bangladesh, with most moving to neighbouring India, the owners said, a shift that represents a major blow to a key pillar of Bangladesh’s economy and could extend beyond the current unrest.

Industry leaders have said rising wages, energy shortages and political uncertainty have weakened the low-cost advantage that helped ‌make Bangladesh the world’s second apparel exporter after China, prompting global brands to diversify sourcing.

The protests have caused more than $400 million in production losses, according to the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA), in an industry that accounts for more ‌than 80% of Bangladesh’s export earnings and nearly 40% of its manufacturing jobs.
India has emerged ‌as ⁠the biggest beneficiary, while buyers are also looking to Vietnam, Cambodia and Indonesia to reduce supply-chain risks and improve delivery ⁠reliability, industry leaders said.
Those pressures intensified on Wednesday when Bangladesh approved a 36% increase in the minimum wage for garment workers, the smallest rise in four decades.

The increase fell well short of workers’ demands to more than double wages, triggering fresh clashes with police even as Abdur Rahman Tarafder, secretary of the Ministry of Labour and Employment, ​said the wage increase was “satisfactory” and that he hoped all ‌workers would resume work from Saturday.
Industry leaders said the increase would nevertheless narrow Bangladesh’s labour-cost advantage over India, although union groups argue the wages remain low by global industry standards.
Babul Akhter, a union leader and workers’ representative on the government-appointed wage board, said brands should not use the unrest to justify shifting orders out of Bangladesh.

He said retailers already factor political instability and labour ‌unrest into sourcing decisions, making such moves “hard to justify” and raising “serious doubts” whether the unrest was more than an excuse.

Instituted in the name of the late Smt. Kalyani Venkataraman to mark the 101st birth anniversary celebrations of Dr. Mrs. YGP, the award was presented by Rtn. Ravi Venkataraman.

Mr. Sivakumar and Kalaimamani Bombay Gnanam, renowned theatre and film writer, director, and producer, felicitated the awardee during the ceremony.
